why: Grant Wood wrote in 1941 that the woman is the farmer's grown-up daughter (his sister Nan said the same); Britannica also calls them farmer and daughter. Card statement (wife) is false.

Concrete-like materials predate Rome (Tiryns floors, Nabataeans), which the body already says, but the Romans were the first to use concrete extensively (from c. 300/150 BC; Pantheon, Colosseum). The open wording with 'extensively' is unambiguous without the options.
Sudan has the most pyramids: Wikipedia counts about 255 Nubian pyramids, Sky HISTORY 'more than 200' (vs about 100-140 in Egypt); 'over 200' and 'about 255' agree.
changes: a0570 notes: added that pyramid counts vary (over 200 to about 255) and Mesoamerican platforms are not counted.

why: The nickname 'powerhouse of the cell' (Siekevitz 1957) belongs to the mitochondrion. Only the card's explanation overstates ('unique' own DNA: chloroplasts have DNA too), which the body already treats correctly.
Goethe himself wrote the Urfaust (c. 1772-1775, Frankfurt); it survives in Luise von Göchhausen's copy, published by Erich Schmidt 1887. Herder had nothing to do with it; statement false.

The card asks for a CONTINENT; the bank answered with a region. The classic 'cradle of civilisation' is Mesopotamia, a region of West Asia, so the answer is Asia; other cradles (Nile valley in Africa etc.) and the 'cradle of humankind' (Africa) are noted.
changes: f12094 corrected in place (its only wording): answer Mesopotamia -> Asia/Asien/Азия; w12222 reworded to the card's continent question narrowed to the classic sense, cardText set to the card's words; new answer sentence in all three bodies; spans, source, article notes updated.

why: In constitutional usage a Staatenbund is a Konföderation, while Föderation means Bundesstaat, so the card statement is false; but Duden also glosses 'Föderation' loosely as any alliance of states (incl. Staatenbund). The open question's answer Konföderation is right either way.
changes: a1855 notes: added the Föderation/Konföderation distinction and Duden's loose usage.

why: The 1000th Tatort (13 Nov 2016, NDR, Lindholm and Borowski) was titled 'Taxi nach Leipzig' like the first episode of 1970, not 'Taxi aus Berlin'.

answer: Mucus (saliva thickened by the mucin MUC5B)
why: BBC Science Focus: exercise raises salivary protein, 'especially a kind of mucus called MUC5B', making saliva thicker and harder to swallow, 'so we spit it out'; Ligtenberg et al. 2015 measured the MUC5B rise. What is spat is thick saliva; 'thick, protein-rich saliva' is already accepted in the notes.
Joseph Pilates was born 9 Dec 1883 in Mönchengladbach (Prussia, German Empire); no source links him to Poland. Statement false.
Meissen manufactory founded 1710 (decree 23 Jan 1710), Europe's oldest; Sèvres began as Vincennes 1740 and moved to Sèvres 1756. Statement false.
The Sachertorte is a chocolate cake with apricot jam and a chocolate glaze (de.wikipedia; Austrian ministry of agriculture's traditional-food register). Statement 'no glaze' false.
The first German broadcast (29 Oct 1923, Vox-Haus) opened with a cello solo with piano, Kreisler's 'Andantino in the style of Martini' (Otto Urack, Fritz Goldschmidt), not Goethe's Faust.

De Telegraaf is a Dutch (Amsterdam) daily, not Danish, so the statement is false. But it is no longer clearly the largest: NOM figures give the Algemeen Dagblad the larger readership since 2020, so 'is the best-selling daily' was outdated.
changes: w11630 reworded (en/de/ru) to 'In which country is De Telegraaf published, for decades its best-selling daily?'; a2255 notes on the AD overtaking it.

why: Siebenbürgen is simply the German name of Transylvania (one region); only the wider Romanian usage of 'Transilvania' sometimes adds Banat, Crișana and Maramureș. Statement false.

Catullus 37/39 mocks the Celtiberian Egnatius for brushing his teeth with urine as a Celtiberian custom; Diodorus 5.33.5 and Strabo 3.4.16 attribute it to Celtiberians/Cantabrians. Our wording already asks about the Celtiberians and the card's Roman premise is corrected in notes.

Rome is usually named the first city of a million (1st century AD, Kolb); Wikipedia notes Rome, Jiankang or Chang'an may have been first and estimates vary. Our 'usually named' wording and notes cover this; the card's 133 BCE date is not in our wording.
The GDR lowered majority to 18 by a law of May 1950; the Federal Republic only from 1 Jan 1975 (Bundestag vote 22 Mar 1974, law of 31 Jul 1974). Statement false.

Napoleon is the figure German Jews regarded as the forerunner of emancipation (ghettos opened, equality in French-ruled German lands), but his 1808 'Infamous Decree' restricted Jews in France; Hardenberg's Prussian edict of 1812 also granted Jews greater freedoms (citizenship, with reservations). The printed answer is unknown, so both count.
changes: a2377 bodies: overstated 'no European ruler did more' sentence replaced by 'best known for …', adding the 1808 decree and the 1812 Prussian edict under Hardenberg; f12407 spans moved; notes accept Hardenberg.

why: Arlene Phillips created the original roller-skating choreography of Starlight Express (London 1984) and is credited for Bochum; Pina Bausch had nothing to do with it.

Wikipedia: in 2005 Golf Digest ranked Scotland first for golf courses per capita (countries under 500,000 excluded); another write-up of Golf Digest's list (dated 2007) also has Scotland first. Saudi Arabia appears in no such ranking.

DIN 477 prescribes left-hand outlet threads for fuel/flammable gases (propane, butane, hydrogen, acetylene …); non-flammable gases such as argon, CO2, nitrogen and oxygen use right-hand threads. Statement 'all' false.

Molt onset in snowshoe hares is timed by photoperiod and does not shift with snow; snow only modulates the rate (Mills et al. 2013 PNAS; Zimova et al. 2018). The body already corrects the card's 'earlier winters' to shorter snow seasons.
